fields.title: Tyaga: Too Few Clients for A/B Testing
fields.summary: The team wants to test a hypothesis via experiment, but the sample size will never be enough. Decide how to validate.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you validate this hypothesis given this client count?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Tyaga.
fields.brief/company: Tyaga is a fictional B2B fleet management service: 400 client companies, each with 5 to 300 vehicles. Annual subscription.
fields.brief/context: The team proposes adding automated maintenance scheduling instead of a manual calendar. Six weeks of engineering work. A developer suggests rolling it out to half the clients as an A/B test to compare renewal rates. Renewals happen once a year, on each client's specific anniversary date.
fields.brief/objective: Determine whether to build this feature without wasting six weeks.
fields.brief/constraints: Three developers, one designer. Three weeks remain until next quarter's planning.
fields.brief/task: Decide how you will validate the hypothesis and justify your approach.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: When A/B testing is impossible, validation is not canceled
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A small client count does not mean deciding blindly. It means choosing a metric closer to the action—one occurring weekly rather than annually—and leaning on lightweight tools as primary methods rather than secondary ones. A prototype answers "will they understand it," feature flag toggling answers "do they need it," and early access yields qualitative feedback faster than any test. And the clearest signal of what to build is usually already sitting in support tickets.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
400 clients. Renewal is a once-a-year event per client, totaling roughly 33 renewals per month across the entire base.

Current renewal rate: 87%. To confidently detect an increase to 91% at this baseline, roughly 1,400 observations per variant are required.

The analyst stated flatly: "At 33 renewals a month split across two variants, that's seven years. An A/B test on renewal rate is fundamentally impossible for us, and won't become possible under any growth we are planning."

There are higher-frequency metrics: 78% of clients visit the maintenance section at least once a week; overdue maintenance visits average 4.2 per fleet per month.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
The idea was brought up by the CTO in a meeting, taking up forty out of sixty minutes. There was no written prep; out of four ideas voiced, three were proposed by him and the head of support.

Rationale: 11 tickets over the quarter saying "missed maintenance, vehicle broke down."

Meanwhile, support holds another data point not mentioned in the meeting: 60 tickets in the same quarter complaining that the maintenance calendar cannot be populated in bulk—users have to enter vehicles one by one.

The fourth idea, from the analyst—"show overdue maintenance list on the home screen"—was not discussed.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
From the team:

Automated maintenance scheduling—six weeks, touches telematics integration.
Bulk calendar upload—four days.
Overdue maintenance list on home screen—two days.
Clickable prototype of automated scheduling—one day, interviewing five clients—two more days.

Separately: the "fuel consumption reports" section has been debated for six months regarding its necessity. It is used by 9% of clients. Toggling it off for 20 clients for two weeks takes one hour of work.

You have 12 clients who historically agree to early access and provide detailed feedback.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: How It Was Decided Last Time
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
A year ago, there was a similar debate over the waybills module. They decided to "build and see": rolled it out to everyone, and a quarter later renewal rates grew from 84% to 87%.

The gain was attributed to the module. Later it turned out that in the same quarter, pricing tiers changed, two most dissatisfied clients churned, and the account manager was replaced.

Attributing the increase to any single factor proved impossible, and the debate over the module's value continues to this day.

In the post-mortem, they wrote: "next time we need a control group." How exactly to get one with 400 clients was never discussed.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Assemble a validation plan from cheap methods
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Acknowledge that A/B testing renewals is impossible, pick a proxy metric closer to daily usage, test comprehension via prototype with early-access clients, settle the old fuel report debate via feature flag toggle, and build a 4-day bulk-upload version before committing to six weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The prototype test with five early-access clients yields an unexpected finding: three out of five do not want full automation because they distrust telematics data and fear maintenance will be scheduled at the wrong time. This doesn't kill the idea, but transforms it—they need automated suggestions requiring human approval, not fully autonomous booking.
Bulk calendar upload launches in four days; manual entry support tickets drop from 60 to 7 per quarter. This was the largest volume complaint, yet went unmentioned in the meeting.
Toggling off fuel reports for 20 clients results in only 2 tickets over two weeks—closing a six-month debate.
Automated scheduling moves to the next quarter recast as "suggest and confirm," with its success metric defined as overdue maintenance visits per fleet per month rather than renewals.
Trade-off: you didn't build the headline feature this quarter, and the CTO viewed this as procrastination.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Run the A/B test on half the clients anyway
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Split the client base in half, roll out automated scheduling to one half, and compare renewal rates after one year.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
After six weeks, the feature is ready and the base is split.
After a year, the difference in renewal rate is 1.2 percentage points, within a margin of error estimated by analytics as ±5. No conclusion can be drawn—a fact known before launch, since accumulating the required sample size takes seven years.
During this year, half the clients lived without a feature that the other half found useful, and three wrote complaints about it.
Trade-off: you spent six weeks of dev time and a year of waiting on a test whose result was predictably statistically indistinguishable from zero.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Clients are few and reachable. Send out a survey asking whether they need automated maintenance scheduling and if they would use it.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
96 out of 400 clients respond. 71% say the feature is needed, and 64% say they would use it.
The feature is built over six weeks. Two months later, 12% of clients use it.
During post-mortem, the team discovers what a 3-day prototype test would have shown: people distrust telematics data and don't want maintenance scheduled without confirmation. The survey didn't capture this because it asked about stated intent rather than actual operational risk.
Trade-off: you cheaply obtained strong agreement that predicted absolutely nothing.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Build it and compare before vs. after
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Roll out to everyone and observe how overdue maintenance visits and renewal rates change compared to last quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The feature launches six weeks later. Overdue maintenance drops from 4.2 to 3.1 per fleet per month—a noticeable change.
Renewal rate cannot be meaningfully evaluated: there were only 100 renewals during the quarter, and variance exceeds the effect size.
The debate over causation repeats exactly like a year ago with waybills: in the same quarter, Support launched an email campaign with maintenance reminders, leaving no way to isolate cause and effect.
Trade-off: you chose a high-frequency metric, but once again left yourself without a control group—the exact mistake documented in your last post-mortem.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Considering the first idea mentioned instead of evaluating multiple options
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Idea selection is determined by who proposed it
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Evaluating a solution as a monolithic block instead of testing its independent parameters
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A hypothesis lacking magnitude or mechanism—it cannot be disproved
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Ideas are compared solely on expected upside, ignoring the cost of inaction
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Next steps for each potential outcome were not defined in advance
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Sample size and timeline were not calculated before launch, monitoring results ad-hoc
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: An expensive test was chosen where a prototype or feature flag toggle would have sufficed
